title: Jelly Roll Morton's lack of a following among blacks
summary: Barker says Morton moved around too much to build a following, unlike bandleaders who stayed in one spot, and describes his confident manner.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Do you, do you think that, that Jelly Roll Morton had the wide popularity among blacks that Louis Armstrong did when he was alive?

Never, never, never, never. Jelly, Jelly played in, clubs, and he made records that were popular, but to actually have, he moved around too fast. See, if he just stayed like, in Chicago, and worked in clubs, they stationary, like you make a reputation in the town, like Fletcher Henderson was in New York, Cab Calloway were in New York at the Cotton Club, Fletcher at the Roseland, you heard him on the radio, Duke was at the Cotton Club, you heard him on the radio, Earl Hines in, in the Grand Terrace in Chicago for a period of eight to ten years, you understand? Standard, Chick Webb, Savoy, Borrow for six, seven, eight years, you dig? When you stay in a spot in the town, then you get a following, but Jelly played in Chicago, I don't know how many big spots he played, then he moved out maybe to Wisconsin, and take a group and go to Kansas City and stay here, then he go to California, he was everywhere, so his records were popular, and his music, his songs, lasted, but far as him having a following of, of saying, well I got, you know, everybody, like when he come to New York, he was lost because, nobody knew Jelly in New York, you know, like a personal thing, to have a charisma, and people flock to you, seeing what his, his attitude, you know, he was sharp, you know, and he, he wasn't the guy that, uh, give you a whole lot of thank you, you know, thank you for signing all this, now you're going to hear something, you see, he's, he's, pretty arrogant guy, wasn't he?
